title: Welcome Ambassador
subtitle: Be the first hello a newcomer remembers.
description: Be the first warm face new visitors and guests encounter. Orient newcomers at community events, answer questions, and help them feel at home in the village.
impact: Every visitor who feels welcomed is a potential member of this community for life.
story: Most people decide how they feel about a place within their first hour there. Ambassadors shape that hour. You turn a nervous arrival into someone who knows three names, where things are, and what happens next. Years later, people still tell the story of who welcomed them.
firstStep: At the next gathering, introduce yourself to one person you have never met and walk them to wherever they are headed.
steps: Pick an upcoming event from the calendar and plan to arrive early.
Greet newcomers as they arrive: learn their names, offer water, show them the essentials.
Answer their questions honestly, and note the ones you could not answer.
Before you leave, introduce each newcomer to a member who shares one of their interests.
deliverable: A few lines on who you welcomed and one thing that would make the next arrival smoother.
tips: Name tags feel small until you watch someone relax because they can read the room.
The question under most questions is: where do I fit here? Answer that one.

title: Food Forest Tender
subtitle: Learn the land by feeding it.
description: Assist with planting, pruning, weeding, and harvesting in a food forest or community garden. Learn regenerative growing practices hands-on.
impact: Grows food people can eat, and the living soil that keeps growing it.
story: A food forest is a pantry and a long promise: a tree planted this season feeds people who have not arrived yet. Tending one puts your hands in the daily work of regeneration, and most growers love to teach. Aim to leave every session knowing at least one new plant.
firstStep: Walk a garden or food forest near you and photograph three plants you cannot name yet. Bring the photos to your first session.
steps: Find out when the next tending session runs, or agree one with whoever keeps the garden.
Show up with water, sun cover, and closed shoes, and ask ahead which tools to bring.
Work alongside whoever leads the session: planting, pruning, weeding, or harvesting, whatever the season asks.
Log what you worked on so the next tender knows where things stand.
deliverable: Photos from your session and a note on what you planted, pruned, or harvested.
tips: Morning sessions beat the heat.
Ask why before you cut. Every pruning choice is a small design decision.

title: Potluck & Celebration Organizer
subtitle: Feed fifty people and watch a village happen.
description: Plan, coordinate, and host community potlucks and seasonal celebrations. Handle logistics, theme-setting, and the little touches that make gatherings memorable.
impact: Community bonds form strongest over shared meals and joy.
story: Shared meals are where a village becomes real: friendships start, plans take shape, and the week's tensions dissolve over someone's grandmother's recipe. Hosting one well is logistics in service of joy. You set the table, and the people who come do the rest.
firstStep: Pick a date with the events calendar and write one sentence describing the gathering's theme.
steps: Choose the date, place, and theme, and ask two or three people to plan it with you.
Invite widely: the board, the feed, and personal asks each reach different people.
Coordinate who brings what, plus setup and cleanup crews.
Host the evening: welcome people, open the meal, and let the theme do its work.
Close the loop: thank the helpers and note what to repeat or drop next time.
deliverable: A short recap with photos: who came, what was shared, what you would repeat.
tips: A visible welcome table saves every late arrival.
Plan the cleanup crew before the event, never during.

title: Trail Builder & Maintainer
subtitle: Open the paths that stitch the land together.
description: Help create, mark, and maintain walking trails across the land. Includes clearing, signage, and stewardship.
impact: Connects the land and makes it accessible for all beings.
story: Land only feels like one place when you can walk it. Trails decide what people see, where they linger, and which corners of the land get loved. Building them is honest outdoor work with a result you can walk on the same day.
firstStep: Walk a trail or a path people already use, end to end, and note the two spots that most need attention.
steps: Agree your section and the season's priorities with whoever looks after the land.
Clear, grade, and mark the route as agreed, with care for what grows beside the path.
Add or repair signage so a first-time walker never has to guess.
Report the finished section with photos so the next walker can find it.
deliverable: Before and after photos of your section and a note on any signage added.
tips: Water always wins. Route around drainage from the start.
Wear gloves you trust.

title: Circle Scribe
subtitle: Keep the village's memory.
description: Document meetings, proposals, decisions, and community knowledge. Keep a living record of how the village governs and creates together.
impact: Institutional memory is what makes governance last across generations.
story: Decisions fade, notes last. The scribe turns an evening of discussion into a record the whole village can trust: what was decided, who carries it, and why. Governance outlives any single founder only when someone writes things down well.
firstStep: Read the notes from the last two meetings, if any were kept, and list what a newcomer would still not understand.
steps: Join a meeting and capture proposals, decisions, and owners as they land.
Write the notes the same day, while the nuance is fresh.
Publish them where the village keeps its records, and link any proposals they reference.
Flag open questions clearly so the next meeting starts where this one ended.
deliverable: A published set of meeting notes: decisions, owners, and open questions.
tips: Record decisions and reasons, never the play by play.
Put a name next to every action. Unowned actions dissolve.

title: Village Photographer & Storyteller
subtitle: Show the world what daily life here looks like.
description: Document life here through photos, short videos, and written stories. Capture real days, for the village's own record and for the people who might join it.
impact: Honest stories are how the right people find a village.
story: The people meant to find a village find it through honest pictures of real days: muddy boots, full tables, work in progress. Documentation is also a gift to the future, because a village will want to remember what its early years looked like. Your eye becomes part of that record.
firstStep: Spend twenty minutes photographing one everyday scene, then pick the single frame that tells it best.
steps: Choose a rhythm: an event, a work day, or a week of small moments.
Shoot what actually happens. Real beats staged every time.
Ask before photographing people up close, always.
Edit a small set: five strong images beat fifty loose ones.
File your set where the village keeps its pictures, and share one to the feed.
deliverable: A small edited set, filed where others can find it, and one image or story shared to the feed.
tips: Golden hour flatters the land.
Caption with a sentence of context. Future you will be grateful.

title: Children's Play Day Facilitator
subtitle: Give the kids a wild morning.
description: Co-design and run a Children's Play Day: wild games, nature crafts, story circles, and the kind of unstructured time kids rarely get.
impact: Children who grow up loving a place grow up to look after it.
story: A Play Day is open time: nature crafts, story circles, mud, and the kind of room childhood runs on. The children who grow up loving the land are the ones who will tend it decades from now. A morning of play is land stewardship wearing a silly hat.
firstStep: Ask two children you know what they would do with a whole free morning outdoors, and write down their answers.
steps: Co-design the morning with another facilitator: one anchor activity, lots of open space.
Gather materials the day before and walk the play area for hazards.
Run the morning with more listening than directing. Follow what catches on.
Wrap with a story circle, and send families home with one photo or keepsake.
deliverable: A short recap of the morning: what you ran, what the kids invented, and a photo if families agreed.
tips: Plan half of what you think fits. Play fills the rest.
A snack table prevents most meltdowns.

title: Tech & Platform Steward
subtitle: Keep the digital village standing.
description: Help maintain and improve the village's digital tools: this platform, its forms, and the other tools members use. Bug reports, UX improvements, documentation, and light development.
impact: Helps the village reach people who have not found it yet.
story: A platform is village infrastructure the same way a water system is: invisible when it works, everyone's problem when it breaks. Stewarding it means bug reports that name the actual problem, small fixes that ship, and documentation the next person can follow. Quiet work, long reach.
firstStep: Use the site for ten minutes as a newcomer would and file the first paper cut you hit, with steps to reproduce.
steps: Pick up an open issue, or file the ones you find.
Reproduce before you fix: a bug you can trigger twice is half solved.
Ship the smallest change that solves it, and write down what you changed.
Leave the docs better than you found them.
deliverable: A link to what you shipped or filed: the fix, the report, or the docs.
tips: Small changes get reviewed. Big ones get postponed.
Screenshots turn a vague report into a fixable one.

title: Healing Arts Practitioner
subtitle: Offer your practice.
description: Offer wellness sessions to community members: yoga, meditation, somatic practices, massage, or another healing modality you are trained in.
impact: Wellbeing is regenerative. When people are well, the village thrives.
story: A village that works hard needs places to be worked on. Sessions from trained hands, whether yoga, somatics, massage, or ceremony, keep the people well who keep everything else going. Offering your modality here turns your training into village wellbeing.
firstStep: Write a three sentence description of the session you want to offer: what it is, who it serves, what to bring.
steps: Confirm your offering, and any space or equipment it needs, with whoever arranges gatherings.
Schedule the session and post it where members look for gatherings.
Hold the session with clear consent and comfort agreements up front.
Gather a word of feedback after, and log the session.
deliverable: A note on the session you held: attendance, how it went, whether it should recur.
tips: Small and recurring beats big and once.
Clear agreements up front make deeper work possible.

title: Infrastructure Builder
subtitle: Build the bones of the village.
description: Support construction, repair, and improvement of shared infrastructure: composting systems, water catchment, a communal kitchen, raised beds, fencing, and more.
impact: Built systems are the skeleton the village lives inside.
story: Compost systems, water catchment, raised beds, fencing: built systems are the skeleton everything else hangs on. This work rewards people who like problems you can touch. What you build this month gets used every day for years.
firstStep: Ask whoever is leading a build what the next blocked task is waiting on.
steps: Join a build day and get briefed on the project by whoever leads it.
Work the task with the crew: measure twice, lift with friends.
Photograph what got built and note any materials running low.
Flag anything unsafe or unfinished before you leave the site.
deliverable: Photos of the day's progress and a note on materials or blockers for the next crew.
tips: The person who tidies the tool shed is everyone's favorite builder.
Ask about load paths before improvising a fix.

title: Arts & Mural Maker
subtitle: Paint what words miss.
description: Create art that lives in the village: murals, sculptures, fiber works, installations. Bring beauty to shared spaces through your medium.
impact: Beauty communicates what words can't. This is how a village speaks.
story: Beauty is how a place speaks. Murals, sculpture, fiber, and installations turn shared walls into shared meaning, and they outlast every meeting about how the village should feel. Bring your medium. The village brings the walls.
firstStep: Walk the shared spaces and photograph the one surface that most wants art. Write a sentence on what belongs there.
steps: Pitch your piece to the people who share the space: sketch, surface, materials, timeline.
Gather materials and prep the surface properly. Prep decides how long it lasts.
Create, and let people watch. Working in public is half the gift.
Seal or weatherproof the finished piece and photograph it.
deliverable: The finished piece in place, photographed, with a title and a line about it.
tips: Sketch approval first saves repainting later.
Kids will ask to help. Let them do a corner.

title: Community Music Circle Host
subtitle: Start the rhythm.
description: Lead or organize regular music circles, drum jams, singing circles, or informal concerts. Music is how a village celebrates, grieves, and stays alive.
impact: Rhythm holds community together in ways nothing else can.
story: Music is how a village celebrates, grieves, and remembers itself. A circle needs no stage and no skill floor: a few instruments, a fire, and someone willing to hold the container. That someone is you.
firstStep: Pick a date and invite three people directly. A circle of four is already a circle.
steps: Set the time and place, and post the invitation to the feed.
Bring or arrange a few shared instruments so nobody needs to own one.
Open simply: a rhythm, a known song, or a round anyone can join.
Read the room and close while the energy is still warm.
deliverable: A note or short clip from the circle: who gathered, what was sung or played.
tips: Percussion is the doorway for shy joiners.
Ending on time is what makes people come back.

title: Security & Night Watch
subtitle: Watch over the night.
description: Keep watch at night as part of a safety rotation: nighttime presence, awareness at the entrances, and care for the boundary between the village and the wider world.
impact: Collective safety is how all other contributions stay protected.
story: Every open-hearted place needs people who mind the edges. Night watch is quiet, real responsibility: presence at the entrance, eyes on the boundary, care for everyone sleeping inside it. The village rests because someone is awake.
firstStep: Walk the boundary once in daylight with someone who knows it, and agree the points a round should check.
steps: Agree a rotation slot with the others keeping watch, and get a handover briefing.
Walk the rounds on schedule: entrances, common spaces, boundary points.
Log anything unusual, and wake the right person for anything urgent.
Hand over clearly at the end of your shift, with notes for the next watch.
deliverable: Your completed shift log with any observations passed to the next watch.
tips: A good flashlight and warm layers turn the shift from endurance into ease.
Most of the job is being visibly, calmly there.
